definition: Maxim means a short saying expressing a rule of conduct.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word maxim. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know maxim should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her tennis coach owns exactly one maxim — 'Play the point, not the score' — and applies it to everything from serves to algebra.
A catchphrase is sound with stickiness and nothing more — fun to repeat, empty of instruction, the far end of the line from a maxim's usable rule.
A slogan stops short of a maxim — it rallies you to a brand or a cause for a season, while a maxim hands you a rule of conduct that outlives its coiner.

A proverb is folk wisdom with the author worn away — everybody's saying, describing how life tends to go. A maxim reads like marching orders instead: a rule of conduct you could act on this minute. A proverb observes the world; a maxim tells you what to do in it.

An adage is an old saying grown respectable simply by surviving — age is its credential, and it may only observe. A maxim earns its keep by usefulness instead: however young, it compresses a rule of conduct into a sentence you can act on.

maxim: A slogan stops short of a maxim — it rallies you to a brand or a cause for a season, while a maxim hands you a rule of conduct that outlives its coiner.
The head chef at Marrow keeps a single maxim taped inside every station: 'Taste before you send.' It is not decoration.
New cooks learn fast that the four words are a working rule, applied a hundred times a night, from the sauce pot to the pastry bench.
When a reviewer once asked where the line came from, the chef shrugged and said she had made it up during a disastrous first year.
That answer surprises people who expect kitchen wisdom to be old, handed down through generations of chefs.
But the line earns its place the only way a maxim can — by being usable, every single shift, by anyone holding a spoon.
